You are spot on suspecting the hardware—this machine is definitely hitting its performance ceiling.

The Release Year

The Dell Inspiron 22-3265 All-in-One was rolled out in 2016. The AMD A8-7410 processor inside it was launched just a bit earlier, in mid-2015. Running a modern computing environment on a decade-old entry-level processor is exactly why it feels incredibly sluggish right now.

Why is it so slow?

Your suspicion about the RAM is highly accurate, but it is actually a two-part bottleneck:

  • The RAM Bottleneck: While it has 8 GB of installed memory, the system specs show only 6.94 GB is usable. The missing 1 GB is being permanently allocated to the integrated AMD Radeon R5 graphics card. Running modern Windows 10 with under 7 GB of usable DDR3 RAM forces the PC to constantly shuffle data out of the memory.
  • The Hidden HDD Bottleneck: Because the RAM fills up instantly, the computer is likely leaning heavily on its hard drive to swap active memory data (paging). Based on the 932 GB total capacity shown in your storage settings, this machine almost certainly shipped with a traditional mechanical 1TB HDD rather than a solid-state drive (SSD). Mechanical drives from 2016 trying to handle modern OS background tasks will choke the system to a crawl.

What are you hoping to use this machine for?

If you just want to eke out a bit more life from it for lightweight tasks, upgrading it to a cheap 2.5-inch SATA SSD would make a night-and-day difference compared to adding more RAM. What's the end game for this setup?

turns.response_html:
Realistically, selling it as-is won't net you very much.

Because of the 2016 entry-level processor and its current speed issues, a functioning Dell Inspiron 22-3265 currently sells on the used market (like eBay) for roughly $45 to $75.

Here is how your options break down:

1. Sell It As-Is ($45 – $75)

  • The Reality: If you sell it online, shipping an All-in-One computer is expensive and risky because of the large glass screen, which eats heavily into that profit. If you sell it locally (Facebook Marketplace/Craigslist), you might get $40 or $50 from someone looking for a cheap kitchen or garage PC.
  • Crucial Step: If you choose this route, make sure to completely wipe the 1TB mechanical hard drive so your personal data isn't left on it.

2. Scrap / Recycle It ($0)

  • The Reality: Drop-off recycling centers or e-waste events typically won't pay you for consumer electronics like this; they just ensure it is disposed of safely. You could pull the 1TB hard drive out first and throw it into a cheap external USB enclosure to use as a slow backup drive, then drop the rest of the shell off for recycling.

3. The SSD Upgrade Route (~$20 investment)

  • The Reality: A brand-new 256GB or 512GB 2.5-inch SATA SSD costs around $15 to $25. Swapping out that spinning mechanical drive for an SSD completely removes the disk bottleneck and breathes massive life back into older hardware.
  • The Verdict: It still won't be a gaming rig or a heavy production machine, but it will boot in seconds instead of minutes and become a perfectly snappy dedicated device for lightweight tasks.

If you decide to save it with a cheap SSD, are you thinking about turning it into a lightweight secondary display, a basic utility terminal, or maybe a dedicated dashboard monitor?
